item.title: Having a Hard Time Changing a Behavior? Here’s Why.
item.description:
Growth Mindset

Having a Hard Time Changing a Behavior? Here’s Why.

Overcoming resistance is the key to changing habits.

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • Resistance blocks us from changing behaviors, but we can overcome it.
  • The change model helps identify the cause of resistance in order to work through it.
  • We've all been successful at changing behavior and can do it again.
  • Change is good, it helps us evolve and be better versions of ourselves.

As I’m writing on this beautiful summer day, the sky is blue, the leaves are green, and the temperature is warm. The topic is on change, which usually corresponds with fall and the changing of the leaves. Self-improvement and growth need not wait for the changing of the season. It should happen when we recognize that we are stuck in a behavior and we want to fix it. People often put off change to a later time, like next week, next season, or the ever-popular New Year's resolution. We often call that procrastination, but it’s actually called resistance.

Resistance is what blocks us from working on the behaviors that we know we should work on. We’re all familiar with the word, but most of us aren’t aware of what causes it. Resistance is caused by being low in one or more of the five elements of change. The change model is a powerful tool in our own growth as well as understanding it in others. Each element either propels us or hinders us in our development. The neat thing about the change model is that we’ve all used it in the past without consciously doing it. Since you’ve already successfully used it, you can now use it to change behaviors that you’ve wanted to change but haven’t yet.

Think about a behavior you’d like to change, like eating better, exercising, quitting smoking, being more positive, changing jobs, being less afraid, etc. It can be a negative or unhealthy behavior you’d like to stop or a positive behavior you’d like to start or improve. As you read about the elements, keep track of which ones you are high in and which ones you are low in. The high ones are good. The low ones are causing the resistance and need to be worked on to raise them. The elements are present: discomfort, emotional security, internalization of responsibility, efficacy, and preferred alternative future. They aren’t in any particular order, but we’ll start with present discomfort.

Present discomfort refers to how uncomfortable we are with the behavior. If we don’t see a problem with it and make excuses for it, then we are low in this element. Even though we don’t like to be uncomfortable, in this case it’s a good thing. When we’re comfortable, we’re more likely to continue with what we are doing. That’s great, except for when we’re comfortable with something we want to or know we need to change.

Emotional security involves getting certain needs from our behavior. If we believe that we can do a different behavior and still feel okay, then we have emotional security regarding that behavior. If we don’t feel that we can be happy because no other behavior will work, then our emotional security is low. It’s important to look at what we get out of the behavior and what we can do instead. Logically, we know this is possible, but sometimes we get stuck in our emotions, and this creates doubt.

Internalization of responsibility is based on who you hold responsible for the behavior. Many people blame negative behaviors on how they were brought up. Once you are aware that a behavior is bad for you, then you have a choice to do it or not. Our upbringing can be a contributing factor, but it’s also a very common excuse. Once you own it, you can fix it. Until then, you make yourself powerless by blaming someone else.

The next element is efficacy. People get this one confused sometimes. Efficacy has to do with one’s belief in one's ability to do something. This is a bit different than their actual ability. Efficacy is more powerful as attitude can propel us past our actual ability. If you’re familiar with The Little Engine That Could, it was the engine’s belief and drive of thinking that he could that got him over the hill. Belief in ourselves and our ability is one of the most powerful tools we can have. Unfortunately, the opposite is also true.

The last element is the preferred alternative future. When you go to change a behavior, it’s important to be able to visualize what you will be doing instead. It’s usually not enough to just say I will or won’t do something, we need to know what we’ll be doing instead and believe that it’s possible and sustainable. When someone lacks a preferred alternative future, they tend to see change as unlikely or unattainable.

Hopefully, you’ve been thinking about the behavior you want to change as you read each element. Which ones are strong and which ones are the weak ones? Resistance has a lot more shape now and is easier to address. The resistance is linked to the elements that you are low in. It’s important to focus on those elements in order to strengthen them. The strong ones can help you develop the weak ones. Once you are strong enough in all five elements, success is right there. Remember, you’ve already done it with other behaviors that you’ve already changed. Having the language helps you be more deliberate in your actions. Change is a good thing and should be embraced, as that is how we improve throughout our lives.

item.title: Can You Love Your Spouse but Want a Divorce?
item.description:
Divorce

Can You Love Your Spouse but Want a Divorce?

Why some marriages end even when love remains.

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • Love can remain even when a marriage ends.
  • Emotional and practical needs that go unmet can create distance.
  • Repeated conflict or broken trust can wear down even the most committed relationships.
  • Diverging values and life goals can lessen compatibility, hastening the end of a relationship.
Source: Soroush Karimi / Unsplash

Not every person who comes to me for a divorce does so because they despise their spouse. There are always those who tell me, in no uncertain terms, that they love their spouse and that’s why they’re leaving them. Or that’s why they decided together to end their marriage. These are the divorces that are often misunderstood by those who witness them from outside the relationship. Counterintuitive, for sure, but there are reasons why you can love your spouse but still want a divorce.

Needs Continue to Go Unmet

One of the quickest paths to feeling lonely in a marriage is not having your needs met. Unmet needs can be emotional, physical, or both. If, for example, your spouse doesn’t communicate well or is simply uninterested in your feelings, whether about the relationship or something you are experiencing unrelated to it, you can feel unsatisfied by the quality of your interactions.

Additionally, not feeling supported at home, such as when gender roles are imbalanced and one spouse is doing all the housework and household planning and bearing the mental load that comes along with it while the other sits back and watches, can result in the overworked spouse not having their needs met.

Then, of course, there are physical needs that can go unmet. Sex can be nonexistent, unsatisfying, or mechanical, which can leave one or both spouses dissatisfied and alone in the relationship. In other words, one unmet need can lead to another.

In all of these examples, love may exist for a partner. However, the love a person feels for their spouse may not, over time, be enough to make up for what’s lacking for them in other areas. At some point, even the most loving spouse can reach their breaking point and want a divorce.

There’s Ongoing Conflict

Whether a couple is fighting over who left the lights on in the bedroom all day or who is always leaving the toothpaste cap off, or it’s something more serious, such as spending beyond what the household budget allows, unresolved conflict can eventually take its toll. This is especially true if one spouse has repeatedly tried to work with the other to resolve their differences, but the other is unreceptive.

Love may remain. However, the continual push and pull, with no end in sight, can become exhausting enough for one or both spouses to resign themselves to being apart despite their feelings for one another.

Values, Priorities, or Goals Have Diverged

Strong marriages are rooted in shared values, priorities, and goals. When those diverge, one or both spouses may feel they are growing apart. Everything can look fine on the outside, and a family could be operating successfully day to day, with the bills paid, dinner on the table at a set time, and the kids well cared for.

However, if the long-term plan has deviated from expectations, it can create dissension between spouses, despite how much they love each other. A lifestyle in which one person’s vision for the future doesn’t match their present and hasn’t for a while can become overbearing and eventually unsustainable. When this happens, one person may decide to pursue a divorce.

Trust Has Been Eroded

This doesn’t have to be caused by something as egregious as an affair. Even small disappointments, where words don’t meet actions, can erode trust between spouses.

If a spouse, for example, agrees to clean the kitchen after dinner or take out the trash and then repeatedly reneges on their promise, their spouse will no longer value their word. This can lead to resentment, anxiety, frustration, and burnout. It can also lead to ongoing arguments, which contribute to the breakdown of the relationship.

In terms of infidelity, some couples do attempt to come back from it. And while repair after an affair is possible, if the offending spouse repeatedly engages in the same behavior or behaviors that give rise to suspicion, it will eventually wear away at any trust that still exists and prevent the rebuilding of it.

Love Isn’t Enough

Even where love exists, it may not be sufficient to carry a relationship when it is plagued by one or both partners’ unmet needs, characterized by daily arguments, challenged by divergent values, priorities, and goals, or compromised by a lack of trust. More than one or all of these characterizations can exist at the same time, even feeding off each other. For love to fuel a couple, it needs to be nurtured. The above behaviors can only deplete it.

Leaving Is an Expression of Care

Not every marriage is meant to last forever, but that does not diminish the value of the time two people shared or the personal growth that came from it. Relationships can change us in lasting ways even when they come to a close. Sometimes, choosing to end a marriage is an expression of care, an acknowledgment that love can take a different form as we evolve.

item.title: Victims Most Vulnerable to Domestic Violence
item.description:
Domestic Violence

Victims Most Vulnerable to Domestic Violence

How the psychology of seclusion increases risk of ongoing domestic abuse.

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • Risk factors within rural areas include attitudes more tolerant of intimate partner violence.
  • Such violence is often more severe and ongoing in remote or rural areas, compared with urban areas.
  • Police collaboration with shelters and safe space for victims facilitate reporting.

Domestic violence occurs all over the world within every type of community. As a career prosecutor, I have dedicated the last 30 years to seeking justice for these victims and holding perpetrators accountable. Yet one of the biggest challenges involved in this area is detection. According to research, there are some types of populations and geographic areas that are more likely to conceal ongoing abuse. Because within relationships of physical abuse, the risk of serious injury or death can increase over time, the goal is to detect and intervene sooner rather than later.

Source: Image by Kev from Pixabay

Behind the Scenes of Seclusion

Susanne J. M. Strand and Jennifer E. Storey (2019) compared the severity of intimate partner violence as well as risk factors in urban, rural, and remote geographic locations by studying risk assessments conducted by Swedish police between 2010 and 2014.[i] They found that rurality was linked with reports of partner violence severity, risk factors, and their relationship to risk judgments.

Strand and Storey explain that, within a country, partner violence frequency is related to population density. Although densely populated urban areas are sometimes believed to be most dangerous, in cases of intimate partner violence, such violence in rural communities is often the same as or greater than in urban areas. They explain that prior research (Logan and colleagues, 2001) found that some risk factors were more prevalent among rural area perpetrators than those in urban areas—such as having more unemployment and less education, and being more likely to use psychoactive medication, often combined with alcohol. Strand and Storey also shared that rural perpetrators were more likely to have prior convictions for partner violence, making them at higher risk for recidivism. They note that other research (Lanier and Maume, 2009) similarly identified unemployment as a risk factor for this in rural areas.

Strand and Storey note that other risk factors within rural areas include attitudes more tolerant of partner violence, which support traditional gender roles and often stem from patriarchal ideology, as well as victim blaming. They recognize that rural victims and perpetrators also have less access to resources that might reduce rates of partner violence, such as transportation or substance abuse treatment, than community members in urban areas.

Remote Areas Facilitate Ongoing Abuse

Strand and Storey’s research found that reports of such violence were higher in remote and rural areas than in urban areas. In studying the specific offenses reported, they also found that victims had experienced violence for longer periods of time. They suggest that limited access to services could explain delayed reporting within these groups, because victims in less populated areas have less access to community services that can help them report abuse. They also note what many victims experience as a practical matter—lack of public transportation to a police station to report a crime, compared with victims in urban areas. Strand and Storey further list lack of access to shelters and health care as factors that can delay reporting because such resources offer protection from an abuser and the chance to escape an abusive relationship. They conclude that limited access to resources in less populated areas may partially explain the heightened severity in such locations.

Bringing Help to Remote Communities

When a partner in a remote area musters the courage to call for help, response speed matters. Strand and Storey suggest that because rural areas contain more severe instances of such violence, police officers in less populated areas should act fast. And even when law enforcement caseloads prevent immediate investigation, perhaps due to more serious cases being in the queue, they point out what many victims already know as a practical matter: having a safe place to stay allows safe reporting even with delayed investigation.

Heightened awareness sparks action. Understanding remote community dynamics can facilitate detection, prosecution, and ideally, prevention.
